title: Apna Apna Bhaagya
author: Jainendra Kumar
tagline: On a beautiful Nainital night a freezing boy is turned away — and "each to his own fate" becomes an accusation, not a comfort.

overview.intro: Jainendra Kumar’s "Apna Apna Bhaagya" ("Each To His Own Fate") is a first-person story that turns a beautiful hill station into a scene of quiet horror. The narrator and his friend meet a barefoot boy of about ten on a cold, foggy night in Nainital. The boy is hungry, has been dismissed from a job and has come seeking work. The friend tries to find him employment through two lawyers, who refuse; the men have no small change to give him. The next morning the travellers hear that a hill boy froze to death by the roadside. The narrator closes with the phrase "apna-apna bhaagya" — and its bitterness is the story’s whole indictment.

learn.title: A beautiful night, and a boy outside it

blocks.text: Jainendra Kumar opens with atmosphere. Nainital at night is cold and foggy and, for travellers with a warm hotel to return to, beautiful. The narrator and his friend are enjoying the hill station when they encounter a boy of about ten, barefoot and inadequately dressed, wandering in the cold. The story’s technique is to hold the two images together: the lyricism of the setting and the reality of the child within it. Beauty does not shelter him; it only makes him more visible and more abandoned.

The boy’s own account is unsentimental. His parents are alive in a village; he left because the family was hungry and his father beat him. He had a job that paid one rupee and leftover food, and he has been turned out of it. Another, older boy who came with him died after being beaten by an employer. None of this is told for sympathy — it is simply what happened, which is what makes it so difficult to read.

learn.title: The friend’s efforts, and the refusals

items: The narrator’s friend takes the boy to two lawyer friends, hoping they will employ him.
The lawyers refuse, saying they cannot trust an unknown child.
The men discuss helping him but discover they have no small change to give.
The friend can only tell the boy to return the next morning about possible work.
The boy leaves into the cold with no food and no shelter, and the travellers return to their hotel.

blocks.text: Every door the story opens is closed again, and each closure has its own respectable reason. The lawyers distrust the unknown child; the men have no small change; the friend can offer only a tomorrow that the boy may not live to see. Jainendra Kumar does not present these people as monsters. They are ordinary, sympathetic even — and the story’s indictment is precisely that ordinary sympathy, without action, lets a child die.

learn.title: The people, and the distances between them

items.meaning: About ten, barefoot, hungry, dismissed from his job; a working child, not an orphan, who freezes to death.
The first-person visitor who records the encounter and recognises, afterwards, what the group failed to do.
Sympathetic enough to seek work for the boy, but ultimately unable to secure immediate help.
Comfortable, well-off men who refuse to employ an unknown child and so close the last door.

blocks.text: The distances in this story are measured in more than miles. The boy has come down from a village economy of hunger and beatings; the travellers inhabit hotels and professions; the lawyers embody a comfortable suspicion of the poor. The narrator stands between the two, close enough to see the boy clearly and honest enough, at the end, to name what that seeing was worth.

learn.title: The morning news and the final phrase

blocks.caption: Comfort and deprivation held side by side
rows: Enjoying the foggy beauty of Nainital
Barefoot, jobless, wandering in the cold
Beauty as shelter for one, exposure for the other
No food, no work, no roof

blocks.text: The next morning, as the travellers are leaving Nainital, they hear that a hill boy froze to death by the roadside. The narrator understands at once whose body it is. His closing phrase — "apna-apna bhaagya", each to his own fate — is not consolation but accusation: it is the excuse the comfortable use to avoid responsibility, spoken aloud so that the reader can hear how hollow it is. The story ends by turning a resigned commonplace into a charge.

learn.title: Themes: poverty, indifference and the excuse of fate

items.text: The boy has living parents but has run away from hunger.
items.note: He is not an orphan — his poverty, not family death, has forced him into the cold, which makes the neglect harder to excuse.

items.text: The lawyers refuse to trust an unknown child.
items.note: Respectable suspicion closes the last employment door, and it is the boy’s poverty that makes him "unknown".

items.text: The men have no small change to give.
items.note: A detail of casual plenty: they can afford a hotel, but not the price of a child’s night.

blocks.text: The story’s themes are poverty and child labour, the indifference of the comfortable, and "fate" as a device for evading responsibility. Beneath them runs the contrast between appearance and reality — a beautiful tourist town concealing a starving child. Jainendra Kumar’s argument is that the boy’s death was not destiny but the predictable outcome of neglect, and that calling it bhaagya is how a society excuses itself.

This story reliably produces a central-idea question and a question on the significance of the ending. In both, resist reading the final phrase at face value. "Apna-apna bhaagya" is spoken with bitterness, and the strongest answers show that the narrator is indicting the very attitude the words describe. Use the contrast between the foggy beauty of Nainital and the boy’s suffering as your main structural evidence.

items: Establish that the boy is a working child with living parents, not an orphan — the tragedy is economic.

figures.caption: Figure: One night, two worlds
figures.description: A split composition. Left: travellers in warm coats enjoying the foggy, lamplit beauty of Nainital at night. Right: the barefoot boy of about ten on the same road, hands empty, with a closed hotel door behind him. A thin fog drifts across both panels, uniting the scene while separating the fates.

figures.caption: Figure: The chain of refusals
figures.description: A left-to-right chain of five closed doors: the boy seeks work → dismissed employer → lawyers refuse to trust him → no small change among the men → only a promise of "tomorrow". Beneath the final link, the next morning’s news: a hill boy frozen by the roadside.

keyPoints: The story is first person: the narrator recounts an encounter that he later understands was a failure to act.
Nainital’s cold, foggy beauty is used ironically — it shelters the travellers and exposes the boy.
The boy is about ten, barefoot and hungry; he has living parents but ran away from hunger and beatings.
His job paid one rupee and leftover food, and he has been turned out of it.
Another older boy who came with him died after being beaten by an employer.
The friend tries two lawyers, who refuse to trust an unknown child; the men have no small change.
Only a promise of "tomorrow" is offered, which the boy may not live to see.
The next morning he is found frozen by the roadside, and "apna-apna bhaagya" becomes an accusation against the comfortable.
examFocus: Central idea: the story indicts social indifference and the habit of calling preventable suffering "fate".
Significance of the ending: "apna-apna bhaagya" is bitter irony — the narrator charges, he does not console.
Contrast question: hold the beauty of Nainital against the boy’s suffering to expose how neglect hides in plain sight.

questions.prompt: Where does the story take place?
questions.explanation: The narrator and his friend are in the hill station of Nainital on a cold, foggy night when they meet the boy.
questions.commonMistake: The hill-station setting is essential — its beauty is used ironically against the boy’s suffering.

questions.prompt: Why has the boy left his village?
options: His family was hungry and his father beat him
questions.answer: His family was hungry and his father beat him
questions.explanation: The boy says his parents are alive but the family had no food and his father beat him, so he left to find work and food.
questions.commonMistake: He is not an orphan — his parents are living, which makes his neglect purely economic.

questions.prompt: What job did the boy lose?
options: A job that paid one rupee and leftover food
questions.answer: A job that paid one rupee and leftover food
questions.explanation: The boy had been working for a rupee and leftover food, and he has been dismissed from it, leaving him with neither wages nor shelter.
questions.commonMistake: Note how small the wage was — it underscores the value of what he has lost.

questions.prompt: Why do the lawyers refuse to employ the boy?
options: They do not trust an unknown child
He is too young to work by law
They have no room for him
questions.answer: They do not trust an unknown child
questions.explanation: The two lawyers decline on the grounds that they cannot trust a child they do not know — respectable suspicion that closes the last door.
questions.commonMistake: Their refusal is based on distrust of the unknown, not on any shortage of money.

questions.prompt: What news do the travellers hear the next morning?
questions.answer: They hear that a hill boy froze to death by the roadside, and the narrator realises it is the boy they met.
questions.explanation: As they are leaving Nainital, the morning report of a boy frozen by the road tells the narrator exactly what their failure to help has cost.
questions.commonMistake: The narrator recognises the boy; the story does not leave the identity uncertain to him.

questions.prompt: How does the friend try to help the boy?
questions.answer: He takes the boy to two lawyer friends hoping they will employ him, but they refuse; the men find they have no small change, and he can only promise work the next morning.
questions.explanation: The friend’s effort is genuine but entirely indirect — it seeks employment through others and ends in a promise rather than in food or shelter for the night.
questions.commonMistake: Do not describe the friend as indifferent; he acts, but his action is insufficient.

questions.prompt: Explain how the story contrasts the beauty of Nainital with the boy’s suffering.
questions.answer: Jainendra Kumar describes the hill station with real lyricism — the cold, the fog, the pleasure of a beautiful night for travellers with a warm hotel awaiting them. Into that scene he places a barefoot, hungry boy of ten with no work and no shelter. The beauty does not mitigate the suffering; it sharpens it, because the same fog that delights the travellers leaves the child exposed. The contrast exposes how easily deprivation hides inside a picture of comfort, and it prepares the reader for the morning’s news that the boy has frozen to death.
questions.explanation: The answer should treat the setting as a deliberate technique: beauty for one party is exposure for the other, and the juxtaposition is the story’s argument about who is protected and who is not.
questions.commonMistake: Do not merely say the setting is "vivid"; explain what the contrast is doing to the theme.

questions.prompt: What does the phrase "apna-apna bhaagya" mean in the context of the story’s ending?
questions.answer: It means "each to his own fate", and the narrator uses it bitterly to expose the excuse by which the comfortable avoid responsibility for a child’s death.
questions.explanation: Rather than accepting the boy’s death as destiny, the narrator invokes the phrase precisely to show how hollow and self-serving such resignation is; it is an accusation, not a consolation.
questions.commonMistake: Never read the phrase as the story’s sincere philosophy — its tone is ironic and condemning.

questions.prompt: Retell the encounter with the boy and show how the story indicts social indifference.
questions.answer: On a cold, foggy Nainital night the narrator and his friend meet a barefoot boy of about ten. He tells them that his parents are alive in a village but the family was hungry and his father beat him, so he left; a job paying one rupee and leftover food has dismissed him, and an older boy who came with him died after an employer beat him. The friend takes him to two lawyers who refuse to employ an unknown child. The men find they have no small change, and the friend can only ask the boy to return the next morning about work. The boy leaves into the cold with no food or shelter, while the travellers go back to their hotel. The next morning, as they leave, they hear that a hill boy froze to death by the roadside. The narrator closes with "apna-apna bhaagya". Through this sequence the story indicts not cruelty but ordinary indifference: every door closed for a respectable reason, every sympathy expressed without money or action, until the excuse of fate covers a death that human help could have prevented.
questions.explanation: The strongest answers name the chain of refusals and then state the indictment clearly: neglect dressed as fate is the story’s real subject.
questions.commonMistake: Do not portray the travellers as villains; the indictment of ordinary, well-meaning indifference is sharper and more accurate.

questions.prompt: The boy’s death is called "fate". Do you agree that it was fate, or could it have been prevented? Discuss.
questions.answer: The story presents the death as entirely preventable, and the narrator’s closing phrase is meant to be heard as an indictment rather than an acceptance. The boy was turned away by employers, refused by lawyers for being unknown, and left unfed by men who simply had no small change; each of these was a human decision that could have gone otherwise. To call it bhaagya is, in Jainendra Kumar’s argument, the comfortable class’s way of dissolving its own responsibility into the weather. A reader today would recognise the same pattern wherever poverty is described as destiny. What the story demands is that we treat such deaths as failures of action and duty, not as the working of fate.
questions.explanation: Take a clear position against "fate", support it with the sequence of avoidable refusals, and show that the title phrase is ironic — the story condemns the very idea it appears to name.
questions.commonMistake: Do not hedge by saying "both are true"; the text’s irony is decisive and should be argued as such.
